structured_output.hypothesis: If wholly soft-bodied organisms are essentially never preserved, then in the fossil record almost all marine animal occurrences belong to taxa with mineralized skeletons, and the wholly soft-bodied phyla (which make up a large share of living animal phyla) are nearly absent.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Using PBDB occurrences of marine Metazoa (Phanerozoic): occurrences assigned to wholly soft-bodied phyla (Nemertea, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Ctenophora, Gastrotricha, Nematomorpha, Rotifera, etc.) are less than 1% of all marine metazoan occurrences, AND occurrences from collections flagged as soft-tissue/exceptional (Lagerstatte) preservation are under 5% of total. Both must hold for the claim to be supported.
structured_output.fail_criterion: Wholly soft-bodied phyla make up 5% or more of marine metazoan occurrences, or soft-tissue-preservation collections make up 15% or more of occurrences; or intermediate values (1-5% and 5-15%) count as inconclusive. Any of the first two refutes the strong claim that no wholly soft organism is preserved.
structured_output.interpretation: Darwin's 'wholly soft' organisms are interpreted as taxa with no mineralized or decay-resistant skeleton (soft-bodied phyla). 'Preserved' means present as body-fossil occurrences. Darwin's absolute wording ('No organism wholly soft can be preserved') is tested as a strong-bias statement: rare, not literally zero, so Lagerstatten occurrences are measured and expected to be a small minority. The second clause (skeletons decaying on non-depositing sea floor) is not directly testable from PBDB; only the proxy that the record is dominated by skeletonized taxa from depositional settings is used, and this is a stated limitation. Modern reinterpretation: Burgess Shale-type Lagerstatten show soft-bodied preservation is possible but exceptional.
